main_message: Gibraltar was fought over for 400 years because of its position and its sea supply, and the modern dispute over the border, the runway and cross-border jobs is the same argument in new form.

claims_doubted.quote: Historians on both sides count fourteen sieges of it, between 1309 and 1783.
claims_doubted.why: There is no agreed count. Counts vary between roughly 12 and 15 depending on what is called a siege, and the 1309 start (Castilian capture from the Moors) is a Spanish-side convention. The title and the claim of 'both sides' agreement rest on Sayer and García Sanz alone, and the script says nothing on how they differ. 1704 is also usually described as a bombardment and landing, not a siege in the same sense.

claims_doubted.quote: Since July 2026, this gate has had no routine checks.
claims_doubted.why: This conflicts with the final chapter, which says the treaty is only 'provisional, pending a European Parliament vote'. Either checks have ended or they have not. Needs one clear, dated statement of what is actually in force.

claims_doubted.quote: Austria, England and the Dutch backed a rival for Spain's crown; France backed Madrid's king.
claims_doubted.why: Compressed to the point of being misleading. Rooke's fleet was Anglo-Dutch, and the capture was in the name of the Archduke Charles. Hesse-Darmstadt's own motives and the attempt on Barcelona first are omitted. Also 'England' in 1704 and 'British' in 1713 are used loosely.

claims_doubted.quote: Almost all of them left.
claims_doubted.why: 'Almost all' is unsourced. Accounts differ on how many stayed; a few residents did remain. The San Roque origin story is also contested (some settled elsewhere in the Campo, e.g. Algeciras, Los Barrios).

claims_doubted.quote: Spain tried to take Gibraltar back from 1704 to 1705, with French troops, and again in 1727. Neither siege took it.
claims_doubted.why: Omits that the 1704-05 siege came very close in places and that the Spanish force's size is not given. Also the 1727 siege is skipped over in a line, which leaves a viewer unable to count 'fourteen' sieges: the video never lists them.

claims_doubted.quote: "without any territorial jurisdiction, and without any open communication by land."
claims_doubted.why: Utrecht Article X is quoted in part. The same article gives Spain right of first refusal if Britain disposes of the Rock. Selective quotation of a treaty needs the full context.

claims_doubted.quote: By autumn, about fourteen thousand men faced the Rock across the isthmus.
claims_doubted.why: No counter given. Figures for the Spanish lines in 1779 vary by source. Also 'fourteen thousand' echoes the 'fourteen sieges' title and risks confusion.

claims_doubted.quote: Scurvy spread, until a Danish ship full of lemons was brought in.
claims_doubted.why: Sourcing needed. The Danish ship story is well known in British accounts, but the date and who brought it are not given.

claims_doubted.quote: Between them, the two sides fired nearly half a million rounds.
claims_doubted.why: No counter and no source. Estimates of rounds fired in the Great Siege vary widely, and the 'between them' sum mixes two incompatible records.

claims_doubted.quote: forty-seven ships of the line by the British count, fifty by the Spanish.
claims_doubted.why: The on-screen Fernández Duro quote says '50 navios' that gathered at Algeciras, which is a gathering, not a number in action on 13 September. Mixes the combined fleet's total with those present.

claims_doubted.quote: By the next morning, all ten batteries were gone.
claims_doubted.why: Overstated. Some batteries were burning overnight and a few were destroyed by Spanish crews on the 14th; the video flattens a night of events into one line.

claims_doubted.quote: More than two thousand attackers were lost, by British and Spanish counts; three hundred and fifty-seven were rescued.
claims_doubted.why: The on-screen card gives 'prisoners included' and a separate 185 'hit by gunfire', which the narration does not mention. Loss figures for 13 September 1782 are commonly given at about 1,500 casualties including prisoners; '> 2,000' needs a precise source and definition of 'lost'.

claims_doubted.quote: Sergeant Ince's thirteen men had cut about eighty-two feet of solid rock.
claims_doubted.why: Precise figures with no source on screen. The tunnelling story (Ince, 1782) is usually told with a different start date and the 'by early July' claim needs a dated reference.

claims_doubted.quote: The Rock was never starved out.
claims_doubted.why: Overstated. Famine was severe until relief arrived in 1781 and 1782 and the garrison's survival depended on Royal Navy convoys. The statement is true only in the narrow sense that it never surrendered.

claims_doubted.quote: The garrison's own records count at least eight hundred and seventy dead.
claims_doubted.why: The on-screen card adds up 333 + 536 = 869, not 'at least 870', and excludes scurvy deaths for 1779-80. Number and wording do not match.

claims_doubted.quote: With Spain's consent, the British blew up the Spanish forts.
claims_doubted.why: Date uncertain (the card itself says Montero gives 1811) and the 'consent' rests on one source. The video chooses the version that suits the British position without noting the disagreement in the narration.

claims_doubted.quote: The fence went up in 1909; Spain has never recognised it as a border.
claims_doubted.why: Unsourced in the narration; the on-screen source (García Sanz) is a Spanish historian and no British statement of the purpose or position is given.

claims_doubted.quote: Today, the tunnels add up to about fifty-five kilometres, more than the roads above ground.
claims_doubted.why: Commonly cited figure but unsourced here; the 'more than the roads above ground' comparison needs a counter (road length in Gibraltar is about 30 km or less).

claims_doubted.quote: On the night of the seventh of November 1942, at least six hundred and fifty aircraft lined the runway.
claims_doubted.why: Unsourced, and 'at least' without a counter. Operation Torch aircraft numbers on Gibraltar are usually given as around 600 with variations by source.

claims_doubted.quote: Gibraltar sends its women and children away.
claims_doubted.why: Evacuation of about 13,000 civilians began in 1940, but the sentence omits the figure and that many were sent to London, Madeira and Jamaica; it is also not clear that Spain's occupation of Tangier is the reason.

claims_doubted.quote: Some four thousand six hundred Spanish day workers were cut off.
claims_doubted.why: Who counted? The figure for 1969 varies by source (commonly about 4,800 to 5,000 Spanish workers). No counter.

claims_doubted.quote: In October 2025, people living in Spain held more than four in ten of Gibraltar's jobs.
claims_doubted.why: Source not named. Compare with the later claim of 'fourteen thousand' jobs and 'fifteen thousand' daily crossers; the numbers do not obviously reconcile and different bodies (HM Government of Gibraltar, UK government, Eurostat) count differently.

claims_doubted.quote: La Línea's unemployment was twenty-eight point six percent: the highest of a hundred and thirteen Spanish cities.
claims_doubted.why: Source and date of counting not given in narration; the phrase 'a hundred and thirteen Spanish cities' implies a ranking by a body that is not named.

claims_doubted.quote: Our read: the rich-looking number partly rests on the other side.
claims_doubted.why: Editorial inference presented as analysis. Output per resident divided by 38,000 residents is a standard measure, and the video's own correction is reasonable, but 'our read' should be flagged as opinion and supported by a figure for the non-resident share.

claims_doubted.quote: The old fence is coming down, but a new one stands a few metres behind it, with about a hundred and fifty metres left open.
claims_doubted.why: Unsourced and unclear. 'Coming down' contradicts 'provisional'; what the 150 m gap is, and who built the new fence, is not stated.

one_sided.quote: Inside, Governor Diego de Salinas had barely a hundred soldiers, by a Spanish count.
one_sided.why: Foregrounds the weakest-garrison figure and attributes it, but the 'up to five hundred' British figure comes later in a flatter sentence. Fine for balance, but the emotional emphasis ('barely', 'refused to surrender') sits with the Spanish version.

Frames the 1704 change as an expulsion without noting that residents were allowed to stay on oath and that many chose to leave out of loyalty to Philip V, or that the Anglo-Dutch force was acting for a rival claimant to the Spanish crown and not for Britain alone.

one_sided.quote: The treaty never mentions the sandy isthmus to the north. Spain says the isthmus was never ceded. Britain says Gibraltar includes it.
one_sided.why: Presented as an even split, but Britain's position rests on the isthmus' use since 1713 and on prescription. The line leaves out that Britain's claim is not accepted by Spain and the issue is still contested in the EU treaty. Slight false symmetry.
Passes quickly over 1727 and the 1704-05 siege with no figure for the Anglo-Dutch garrison or the Spanish loss. A viewer sees only British success.

one_sided.quote: The garrison's answer was heat: cannonballs heated red-hot, so that whatever they hit caught fire.
one_sided.why: Heroic framing ('answer') with no mention of the garrison's own destruction of the town, plunder after 12 April 1781 (touched on later) or the heavy civilian suffering. Compare with the neutral treatment of Spain's 'cut off the food'.

one_sided.quote: Their answer to red-hot shot: ten floating batteries, designed by the French engineer d'Arçon.
one_sided.why: Presents the failure as French hubris. The video includes d'Arçon's request for a test being refused, which is balanced, but does not say who refused it. A viewer will assume Spain; the 1785 source says the council did.

one_sided.quote: The Rock was never starved out.
one_sided.why: Triumphal line that smooths over the near-starvation of 1779-81 that the video itself describes.

one_sided.quote: The garrison's own records count at least eight hundred and seventy dead.
one_sided.why: Placed beside Montero's 'six thousand outside', the garrison's dead look small. The comparison is not like-for-like (Spanish 'all causes' for a bigger force over years) and the video does not say so.

one_sided.quote: With Spain's consent, the British blew up the Spanish forts.
one_sided.why: Leads with consent and omits the consequence: the forts, once gone, left the neutral ground open to British advance. The Spanish reading comes only in the next sentence.

one_sided.quote: In 1908, Britain told Spain, "as an act of courtesy," that it would fence the edge of the neutral ground.
one_sided.why: The British phrase is used without comment. A Spanish listener would hear it as a unilateral act dressed as a courtesy; the narration neither says nor challenges that.

one_sided.quote: For the rest of the war, a Spanish scholar found, Spain protested British ships in its waters, but not the airstrip.
one_sided.why: Used to imply Spanish acquiescence. The silence of a Franco regime that was dependent on Allied goodwill and on food imports is not the same as consent. The video draws no such caveat.

one_sided.quote: Those tunnels became a city inside the Rock
one_sided.why: Admiring tone for the tunnelling, including the claim of British and Canadian tunnellers, with no word on the forced labour of Spanish workers or the civilian evacuation costs.

one_sided.quote: In June 1969, Spain closed the land frontier completely.
one_sided.why: States the closure but does not give Spain's stated reason (response to the 1969 Gibraltar constitution and the UN decolonisation resolutions) or that it cut Gibraltar off for 16 years. Spain is the actor without context.

The 'twist' sequence (La Línea unemployment, Gibraltar's wealth depending on the other side) tilts toward a Spanish-grievance reading. The video could add that Gibraltar also pays social contributions for those workers and that frontier workers choose the jobs.

one_sided.quote: Remember this street? In 2024, La Línea's unemployment was twenty-eight point six percent
one_sided.why: Sets Spanish poverty against Gibraltar's wealth with no comparison to other Campo de Gibraltar towns, or to national figures, and no mention of Spain's own economic policy.

one_sided.quote: The old fence is coming down, but a new one stands a few metres behind it
one_sided.why: Hints that the treaty is cosmetic. Without a source this reads as an insinuation against Britain and Gibraltar.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: The fleet answered with some fifteen thousand rounds.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Who counted the rounds? No source on screen or in narration.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: British accounts put the defenders at up to five hundred, counting armed townsmen.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Source not named. 'British accounts' is vague; the Spanish figure at least names a historian on screen.

casualty_counter_missing.why: Spanish or British count? Not stated.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: Between them, the two sides fired nearly half a million rounds.
casualty_counter_missing.why: Nobody is named as the counter, and the sum of two sides' records is the video's own.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: By September 1782, about seven and a half thousand men held the Rock.

casualty_counter_missing.why: The narration blurs two counts into one. The screen shows '> 2,000 lost, prisoners included' with a separate '185 hit by gunfire before the fires', but 'lost' is not defined (dead, drowned, captured?) and the 357 'British return' is not named in the narration.

casualty_counter_missing.why: The Drinkwater return is on screen but not spoken; 'at least' and the 333 + 536 split are not explained, and the scurvy exclusion is shown only on screen.

casualty_counter_missing.why: Montero is named, but the video does not say these are estimates from memory 77 years later, nor whether 'outside' means Spanish and French.

casualty_counter_missing.why: Who counted, and when? Different sources give different figures.

casualty_counter_missing.quote: The UK government puts the daily crossers at about fifteen thousand.

hard_to_follow.quote: To walk in from Spain, you cross an airport runway.
hard_to_follow.why: Strong image but then it jumps to 1782 batteries and 1941 runways in four lines; a first-time listener has no way to place the dates.

hard_to_follow.quote: Austria, England and the Dutch backed a rival for Spain's crown; France backed Madrid's king.
hard_to_follow.why: The War of the Spanish Succession in one sentence, with no names, is very hard to take in by ear.

hard_to_follow.quote: On the fourth of August 1704, Gibraltar surrendered. English histories say the twenty-fourth of July, on the old calendar.
hard_to_follow.why: A date change heard once is confusing, especially with the number-heavy sentences on either side.

hard_to_follow.quote: Spain tried to take Gibraltar back from 1704 to 1705, with French troops, and again in 1727.
hard_to_follow.why: Dates and sieges pile up, and 'back from 1704' is ambiguous: it reads as if Spain only tried from the moment of loss.

hard_to_follow.quote: At half past nine, the batteries moved into position. At a quarter to ten, the garrison opened fire. At ten twenty-five, by the Spanish account, some four hundred guns answered together.
hard_to_follow.why: Three clock times and a gun count in ten seconds. Listeners cannot hold them, and 'answered together' is unclear: whose guns?

hard_to_follow.quote: Four days later, the French and Spanish fleets sailed in, under the Duc de Crillon: forty-seven ships of the line by the British count, fifty by the Spanish.
hard_to_follow.why: Crillon commanded the army, not the fleet, and the sentence mixes two commanders' roles. The two counts differ by three, and a listener will not know why that matters.

hard_to_follow.quote: From all causes, Montero put the losses near two thousand inside and six thousand outside.
hard_to_follow.why: 'Inside' and 'outside' are not defined for a listener and the next sentence gives a third number that is lower.

hard_to_follow.quote: Which leaves a question the treaty never answered: where does the Rock end?
hard_to_follow.why: Strong line, but the preceding chapter has already made the same point about the isthmus, so it sounds like a repeat.

hard_to_follow.quote: In 1810, with Napoleon's armies heading for the Strait, Spain and Britain were allies.
hard_to_follow.why: Jump from 1783 to 1810 with no word of the Napoleonic alliance or the Peninsular War.

hard_to_follow.quote: That November, Spain's foreign minister called the strip a fait accompli, like the Rock itself.
hard_to_follow.why: 'Fait accompli' and 'like the Rock itself' pack a legal point and a Spanish jibe into a line the listener cannot parse.

hard_to_follow.quote: That divides by the thirty-eight thousand who live there, and leaves out the people in Spain who hold fourteen thousand of its jobs.
hard_to_follow.why: Percentages, pounds and head counts in a row; a viewer who hears 'eighty-five thousand', 'thirty-eight thousand' and 'fourteen thousand' within twenty seconds will lose the point.

hard_to_follow.quote: As of 18 October 2026, the treaty is provisional, pending a European Parliament vote indicated for the fourteenth of December.
hard_to_follow.why: Dated statement mid-flow that contradicts the cold open ('no routine checks'). Ending is also compressed.

top3_fixes: Fix every number so it states who counted it and what is counted (dead, wounded, captured, all causes), and make the narration agree with the on-screen cards: 333 + 536 = 869 and not 'at least 870', explain '> 2,000 lost' and the 185 and 357 figures aloud, and reconcile 'fourteen thousand' jobs with 'fifteen thousand' crossers. Also settle 'no routine checks since July 2026' against 'provisional, pending a vote'.

Fix the structure: cut or tighten the 1704-1730 treaty section and the 'After that, the edge kept moving' stretch, move the subscribe line to the end, and give the 1782 attack a clearer sequence (one clock time, one outcome). Add a short list or map of the fourteen sieges early on, or drop 'fourteen' from the title, since the video never delivers the count it promises.

Fix the balance by adding what is missing on each side: the Utrecht clause giving Spain first refusal, Spain's stated reasons for the 1969 closure, the Anglo-Dutch nature of the 1704 force and the Archduke's claim, the context of Franco's silence on the airstrip, and a British-side source for the 1909 fence. _prompt:
You are a British fact-checker for a history magazine with a background in 18th-century military history. You flag any claim that sounds wrong, overstated or unsourced, any number without a stated counter, and any wording that tilts toward the Spanish side or sneers at Britain.

Below is the complete narration script of a documentary YouTube video titled "Why Gibraltar Was Besieged 14 Times" (about 11 minutes, English narration, animated maps and 3D reconstructions). Lines in [On screen: ...] are text shown on screen at that moment; [silent shot] means picture and music only. Read all of it as yourself and answer honestly. Do not be polite; you have no stake in who made it.

Check especially: (a) factual claims that seem wrong, overstated or missing a source; (b) sentences that favour one side (British or Spanish) by wording, emphasis or omission; (c) any casualty or loss number that does not say who counted it; (d) sentences that are hard to understand when heard once; (e) stretches where you would get bored or leave.

Return ONLY this JSON (no other text). In every "quote", copy the exact words from the script (a short exact phrase is fine):
{"main_message": "<one sentence>",
 "would_keep_watching_after_30s": true|false, "hook_1to10": n, "trust_1to10": n, "balance_1to10": n, "overall_1to10": n,
 "claims_doubted": [{"chapter": "<chapter title>", "quote": "...", "why": "..."}],
 "one_sided": [{"chapter": "...", "quote": "...", "favours": "British|Spanish", "why": "..."}],
 "casualty_counter_missing": [{"chapter": "...", "quote": "...", "why": "..."}],
 "hard_to_follow": [{"chapter": "...", "quote": "...", "why": "..."}],
 "boring_or_slow": [{"chapter": "...", "from_quote": "...", "why": "..."}],
 "top3_fixes": ["<concrete>", "<concrete>", "<concrete>"]}

=== SCRIPT ===
## Midnight at the Gate
Midnight at the Gibraltar frontier. To walk in from Spain, you cross an airport runway.
Since July 2026, this gate has had no routine checks.
The Rock sits at the western gate of the Mediterranean.
Historians on both sides count fourteen sieges of it, between 1309 and 1783.
This is why everyone fought over it, told from both sides' records.
[On screen: "A history explainer · every date sourced · British and Spanish records side by side · Facts as of 18 Oct 2026"]
[On screen: number card "14 sieges · 1309–1783" — "Sayer 1862 · García Sanz 2022 · Gibraltar National Museum"]
In 1782, ten floating batteries came to break it.
In 1941, a runway was laid across the only road to Spain.
So why, today, is the fight over it about paperwork and payrolls?

## 1704: A Rock Changes Hands
Austria, England and the Dutch backed a rival for Spain's crown; France backed Madrid's king.
That summer, their fleet sailed into the Bay of Gibraltar.
Its commanders, Admiral George Rooke and Prince George of Hesse-Darmstadt, came in the name of "Charles the Third."
This plan, printed in 1705, shows the prize: a walled town that historians on both sides would call the key of the Mediterranean.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «la preciosa llave del Mediterráneo» — "the precious key of the Mediterranean" · Sayer, 1862: "the key of the Mediterranean"]
Inside, Governor Diego de Salinas had barely a hundred soldiers, by a Spanish count. He refused to surrender. The fleet answered with some fifteen thousand rounds.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «con cien hombres de guarnición … no había artilleros que las sirvieran» — "a garrison of a hundred men … there were no gunners to serve them"]
On the fourth of August 1704, Gibraltar surrendered. English histories say the twenty-fourth of July, on the old calendar.
British accounts put the defenders at up to five hundred, counting armed townsmen.
Townspeople could stay if they swore loyalty to "Charles the Third." Almost all of them left. By Spanish accounts, most settled a league to the north-east, at San Roque.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «se habia acampado en las haciendas cercanas á la ermita de San Roque» — "had camped on the farms near the hermitage of San Roque"]
In 1713, the Treaty of Utrecht made it permanent: the town, castle and port went to the British Crown, "for ever." But "without any territorial jurisdiction, and without any open communication by land."
The treaty never mentions the sandy isthmus to the north. Spain says the isthmus was never ceded. Britain says Gibraltar includes it.
Spain tried to take Gibraltar back from 1704 to 1705, with French troops, and again in 1727. Neither siege took it.
So in 1730, Philip the Fifth ordered a stone line across the isthmus, out of gun range, to cut Gibraltar off by land. The town behind it is still called La Línea: "the line."
[On screen: Gómez Nadal (Almoraima), on Philip V's order of 8 Oct 1730: «bloquear definitivamente la correspondencia y paso a la plaza por tierra» — "to block, once and for all, all contact with and passage to the town by land"]

## The Great Siege
Half a century later came a different question: can you starve a rock? On the twenty-first of June 1779, Madrid closed every link with Gibraltar.
Spain had joined France in its war with Britain. By autumn, about fourteen thousand men faced the Rock across the isthmus.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «Carlos III declaró la guerra á Inglaterra y se unió á Francia» — "Charles III declared war on England and joined France"]
At sea, from mid-July, a Spanish squadron sealed the port. Its boats at Algeciras had one job: to cut off the food reaching the Rock from Africa.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «encaminado principalmente á privar a la plaza de los viveres que le llegaban de las costas de África» — "aimed above all at depriving the town of the food that reached it from the coasts of Africa"]
By January 1780, thistles, dandelions and wild leeks were daily food for many; an egg cost sixpence.
The governor, General Eliott, could hold the walls. The food had to come by sea.
To break the blockade, Britain sent three relief fleets: 1780, 1781, 1782.
Scurvy spread, until a Danish ship full of lemons was brought in.
On the twelfth of April 1781, the second relief convoy dropped anchor, and Spain's batteries opened fire on the town. The townspeople fled south.
Two days later, soldiers broke into the merchants' stores. A British officer blamed "resentment and intoxication."
Between them, the two sides fired nearly half a million rounds.
By September 1782, about seven and a half thousand men held the Rock.
The garrison's answer was heat: cannonballs heated red-hot, so that whatever they hit caught fire. On the eighth of September, they used them in earnest against the Spanish works.
Four days later, the French and Spanish fleets sailed in, under the Duc de Crillon: forty-seven ships of the line by the British count, fifty by the Spanish.
[On screen: Fernández Duro, Armada española (1901): «alegrando la vista los 50 navios que se juntaron en Algeciras» — "the 50 ships of the line that gathered at Algeciras, a joy to see"]
Their answer to red-hot shot: ten floating batteries, designed by the French engineer d'Arçon. A French account says he'd asked to test them against red-hot shot first. It was refused.
[On screen: Conseil de guerre privé (1785): «l'expérience que l'inventeur avoit demandée … à l'épreuve des boulets rouges» — "the test the inventor had asked for … against red-hot shot"]
The thirteenth of September 1782. At half past nine, the batteries moved into position. At a quarter to ten, the garrison opened fire. At ten twenty-five, by the Spanish account, some four hundred guns answered together. By the next morning, all ten batteries were gone.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «á las diez y veinte y cinco minutos de la mañana … rompieron á un tiempo el fuego» — "at twenty-five past ten in the morning … opened fire all at once"]
More than two thousand attackers were lost, by British and Spanish counts; three hundred and fifty-seven were rescued.
[On screen: number card: "> 2,000 lost, prisoners included — British estimate & Montero (Spain)" · "185 hit by gunfire before the fires — French account, 1785" · "357 rescued — British return" · "Garrison: 16 killed — its own return" {S069} {S070} {S071}]
All that summer, the garrison had also been digging through the north face. By early July, Sergeant Ince's thirteen men had cut about eighty-two feet of solid rock.
In July they blasted a hole for air. A Spanish historian wrote it was big enough for a cannon.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «se formó un boquete tan grande … que pareció bien colocar en el un cañón» — "an opening was made so large … that it seemed right to place a cannon in it"]
The Rock was never starved out. In February 1783, word came of a preliminary peace, and on the fifth, the last shot was fired.
From all causes, Montero put the losses near two thousand inside and six thousand outside. The garrison's own records count at least eight hundred and seventy dead. Gibraltar stayed British.
[On screen: Montero, 1860: «Los últimos sufrieron una pérdida de cerca de dos mil hombres. La nuestra se aproximó á seis mil por todas causas» — "The latter [the besieged] suffered a loss of nearly two thousand men. Ours came close to six thousand, from all causes" · number card: "Garrison return (Drinkwater): 333 killed or died of wounds · 536 died of sickness (scurvy deaths 1779–80 not included)"]

## The Neutral Ground
Which leaves a question the treaty never answered: where does the Rock end? Between the walls and the Spanish line lay a strip of sand: the neutral ground.
In 1810, with Napoleon's armies heading for the Strait, Spain and Britain were allies. With Spain's consent, the British blew up the Spanish forts.
[On screen: Gómez de Avellaneda: «con autorización española, fueran destruidos por los ingleses» — "with Spanish authorisation, they were destroyed by the British" · "Montero gives 1811"]
After that, the edge kept moving. A Spanish historian describes Britain advancing into the neutral zone step by step.

## A Runway on the Isthmus
Why build an airfield on disputed ground? In March 1939, Spain protested that the works stood on "a usurped portion" of its territory.
That November, Spain's foreign minister called the strip a fait accompli, like the Rock itself. Late in 1939, Britain began a hard runway; in 1941, it was laid across the only road to Spain.
[On screen: Spanish government to its London ambassador, 4 Mar 1939 (Marquina Barrio, 1981): «una porción usurpada del territorio nacional» — "a usurped portion of the national territory"]
Then Britain pushed it out into the bay, with stone blasted from the north face and rubble from new tunnels.
Those tunnels became a city inside the Rock: a road about a mile long, a hospital, a power station, dug by British and Canadian tunnellers.
Today, the tunnels add up to about fifty-five kilometres, more than the roads above ground.
This 1943 US Army map shows the town house by house, and the runway reaching into the bay.
June 1940: Spain turns "non-belligerent" and occupies Tangier. Gibraltar sends its women and children away. By 1942, the invasion of North Africa is run from inside the Rock.

For the rest of the war, a Spanish scholar found, Spain protested British ships in its waters, but not the airstrip.
[On screen: Marquina Barrio, 1981: «no queda constancia de reclamaciones por el uso de la pista» — "there is no record of complaints over the use of the strip"]
On the night of the seventh of November 1942, at least six hundred and fifty aircraft lined the runway. The invasion fleets, from Britain and the United States, came through the Strait.

## The Gate
After the war, the argument returned to the gate. In June 1969, Spain closed the land frontier completely.
Some four thousand six hundred Spanish day workers were cut off. The gate fully reopened in 1985.
The same square, today. In October 2025, people living in Spain held more than four in ten of Gibraltar's jobs.
The UK government puts the daily crossers at about fifteen thousand. People on foot still cross the runway.
And on the other side of the gate.
Remember this street? In 2024, La Línea's unemployment was twenty-eight point six percent: the highest of a hundred and thirteen Spanish cities.
Here's the twist. Gibraltar's government puts output per resident at about eighty-five thousand pounds.
That divides by the thirty-eight thousand who live there, and leaves out the people in Spain who hold fourteen thousand of its jobs. Our read: the rich-looking number partly rests on the other side.
In July 2026, Britain and the EU signed a treaty to take the checks off this border.
It says it changes neither side's position on sovereignty. The old fence is coming down, but a new one stands a few metres behind it, with about a hundred and fifty metres left open.
As of 18 October 2026, the treaty is provisional, pending a European Parliament vote indicated for the fourteenth of December.
So why did everyone fight over this place? Where it sits, and the sea that could feed it. A wall in 1704. A line in 1730. A fence in 1909. A runway in 1941.
